market_context: United States/international; U.S. cilantro/coriander terminology contrasted with British and other English usage.
title: Cilantro vs. Coriander: Are They the Same or Different Ingredients?

seo.title: Cilantro vs. Coriander: Same Plant, Different Parts
seo.meta_description: Cilantro and coriander come from Coriandrum sativum. In U.S. English cilantro means the fresh leaves while coriander usually means the dried seeds; naming differs elsewhere.
seo.search_intent: Understand the relationship between cilantro and coriander and how the words change between U.S. and British recipes.

excerpt: Cilantro and coriander come from the same plant, Coriandrum sativum. In U.S. cooking, cilantro usually means fresh leaves and stems while coriander means the dried seed spice; British English often calls the leaves coriander too.
content_html:
Cilantro and coriander come from the same plant, Coriandrum sativum. They are not two species. In U.S. food language, however, the words conveniently separate two very different ingredients: cilantro is the fresh leafy herb, while coriander usually means the dried seeds used as a spice.

That naming rule is regional rather than biological. In Britain and several other English-speaking markets, the fresh leaves are commonly called coriander and the spice is labeled coriander seed. A recipe's country can therefore change what the same word appears to mean.

One plant provides leaves, flowers, seeds, and edible roots

Coriandrum sativum is an annual herb in Apiaceae, the family that also includes parsley, dill, celery, and carrots. Early in growth it produces the green leaves harvested as cilantro. As weather warms and the plant bolts, it flowers and eventually forms the dry fruits commonly sold as coriander seeds.

University extension sources describe cilantro and coriander explicitly as two culinary harvests from the same plant. The roots are also edible and are important in some Thai and other Southeast Asian preparations.

A grower pursuing leafy cilantro often tries to delay bolting, while a grower wanting coriander seed lets the plant flower and mature. Same genetics, different harvest stage.

Fresh cilantro and coriander seed do not taste interchangeable

Cilantro leaves are bright, green, citrusy, and highly aromatic. They are used fresh in salsa, tacos, chutneys, curries, soups, salads, and garnishes, often added late so heat does not drive off too much aroma.

Coriander seeds taste warmer, drier, and more spice-like, with citrus notes but none of the leafy texture. Whole seeds can be toasted; ground coriander appears in spice blends, sausages, pickles, baking, and curries.

That difference is large enough that substituting one for the other rarely works. A teaspoon of ground coriander will not replace a handful of fresh cilantro in pico de gallo, while chopped leaves cannot provide the dry toasted spice character required in a masala.

U.S. and British recipes use the words differently

In the United States, “cilantro” almost always points to fresh leaves and tender stems. “Coriander” without another qualifier usually means the dry seed spice. This split makes ingredient lists easy to interpret once you know the convention.

British recipes typically call the fresh herb “coriander” and specify “coriander seeds” or “ground coriander” for the spice. Someone following a British curry recipe that asks for “a handful of fresh coriander” should buy what a U.S. store labels cilantro.

Other countries and languages add their own conventions. The safest clue is therefore not the word alone but whether the recipe says fresh, leaves, bunch, seeds, whole, toasted, or ground.

The vocabulary can become especially confusing in multilingual recipes. In the United States, “cilantro” almost always points to the fresh leaves and tender stems, while “coriander” usually means the dried seed. In the United Kingdom, “coriander” can refer to the whole plant, with “coriander seeds” added when necessary. Spanish varies by region as well: cilantro is common for the fresh herb, while semillas de cilantro or coriandro may identify the spice. The safest way to translate a recipe is therefore to look at the preparation, not just the noun. A handful chopped over tacos clearly means leaves; a teaspoon toasted and ground for a curry clearly means seed.

How to avoid buying the wrong form

Fresh cilantro is sold as green bunches or packaged leaves and is usually measured by handfuls, cups, sprigs, or tablespoons of chopped herb. Coriander seed is sold whole or ground in the spice aisle and is usually measured in teaspoons.

The objects called coriander “seeds” are botanically dry fruits containing the seed, another example of culinary language choosing convenience over strict morphology. That detail has no practical effect on how the spice is toasted or ground.

The useful conclusion is: cilantro and coriander are the same plant but often refer to different harvested parts. In U.S. English, cilantro means leaves and coriander means seed spice; in British English, coriander can mean the fresh herb too. Read the form and the recipe's regional language before substituting.

faq.question: Can ground coriander replace fresh cilantro?
faq.answer: Not directly. The seed spice and fresh leaves have very different flavor, texture, and culinary roles.

faq.question: What does fresh coriander mean in a British recipe?
faq.answer: It normally means the fresh leaves and stems that U.S. stores label cilantro.

faq.question: Can you eat cilantro roots?
faq.answer: Yes. The roots are used in several Southeast Asian cuisines, particularly in aromatic pastes and marinades.
